line: Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds.
sub: Think cardiac tamponade.
caption:
Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds. It points to cardiac tamponade, where fluid in the pericardium limits ventricular filling and drops cardiac output. Don't forget pulsus paradoxus and electrical alternans on ECG. Definitive fix: pericardiocentesis.

line: Hypercalcemia: stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones.
sub: Kidney stones, bone pain, GI upset, mood changes.
caption:
Hypercalcemia classically shows up as stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones. Most common causes are primary hyperparathyroidism in outpatients and malignancy in inpatients. First line treatment is IV fluids, then calcitonin or bisphosphonates depending on severity.

line: Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability.
sub: Three ways to make a clot.
caption:
Virchow's triad explains thrombosis: stasis (immobility, AFib), endothelial injury (trauma, surgery), and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, factor V Leiden). Almost every DVT or PE risk factor fits into one of these three buckets.

line: Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice, and RUQ pain.
sub: Think ascending cholangitis.
caption:
Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain) points to ascending cholangitis, an infection of the biliary tree from obstruction, often a gallstone. Add hypotension and altered mental status and you have Reynolds pentad, which signals severe disease. Treat with antibiotics and urgent biliary decompression.

line: Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations.
sub: A late sign of raised intracranial pressure.
caption:
Cushing's triad is hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations. It reflects the brain trying to maintain perfusion against high intracranial pressure and often means herniation is near. Think head bleed, mass, or swelling, and act fast.

line: Whipple's triad confirms true hypoglycemia.
sub: Symptoms, a low glucose, and relief with glucose.
caption:
Whipple's triad confirms hypoglycemia: symptoms consistent with low glucose, a documented low plasma glucose at the time, and resolution of symptoms when glucose is raised. If the triad is present in a non diabetic patient, think insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency, or surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use.

line: Wernicke's triad: confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia.
sub: Thiamine deficiency. Give thiamine.
caption:
Wernicke's encephalopathy is the triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency, classically in alcohol use disorder. Most patients do not show all three. Give IV thiamine before or with glucose so you do not worsen it. Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome.

line: Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.
sub: A sympathetic pathway lesion on the same side.
caption:
Horner syndrome is ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side as a lesion in the sympathetic pathway. In the ED, think carotid or vertebral artery dissection, Pancoast tumor, and lateral medullary stroke, especially when it comes with neck pain or headache.

line: High anion gap acidosis: MUDPILES.
sub: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron or INH, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.
caption:
MUDPILES is the classic mnemonic for high anion gap metabolic acidosis: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron or Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates. Start with a good history and check lactate, ketones, and an osmolar gap when a toxic alcohol is possible.

line: Pulsus paradoxus: systolic BP falls more than 10 mmHg with inspiration.
sub: Tamponade, severe asthma, COPD.
caption:
Pulsus paradoxus is a drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mmHg during inspiration. Think cardiac tamponade first, and also severe asthma or COPD exacerbation. During inspiration, increased right heart filling bows the septum into the left ventricle and lowers stroke volume.

line: Kussmaul sign: JVP rises with inspiration.
sub: Constrictive pericarditis, RV infarct, restrictive cardiomyopathy.
caption:
Kussmaul sign is a rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration, the opposite of the normal fall. It means the right heart cannot accommodate extra venous return. Think constrictive pericarditis, right ventricular infarction, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

line: Digoxin toxicity: nausea, yellow vision, and arrhythmias.
sub: Hyperkalemia makes it worse. Treat with DigiFab.
caption:
Digoxin toxicity causes nausea, vomiting, visual changes like yellow halos, and a wide range of arrhythmias, classically atrial tachycardia with block and ventricular ectopy. Acute toxicity raises potassium, and the level predicts mortality. Treatment for serious toxicity is digoxin immune fab.

line: Hyperkalemia on ECG: peaked T waves, then wide QRS, then sine wave.
sub: Give calcium first to stabilize the heart.
caption:
Hyperkalemia progresses on ECG from peaked T waves to PR prolongation, then a widened QRS, and finally a sine wave pattern. If you see ECG changes, give IV calcium first to stabilize the cardiac membrane, then shift potassium with insulin and glucose and albuterol, and remove it from the body.

line: Cullen and Grey Turner signs mean bleeding in the retroperitoneum.
sub: Cullen: around the belly button. Grey Turner: the flanks.
caption:
Cullen sign (bruising around the umbilicus) and Grey Turner sign (bruising of the flanks) point to retroperitoneal hemorrhage, classically severe acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis. They are late and uncommon findings, so their absence does not rule anything out.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Hypocalcemia signs: Chvostek and Trousseau.
sub: Facial twitch and carpal spasm.
caption:
Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability. Chvostek sign is facial twitching when you tap the facial nerve. Trousseau sign is carpal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure for about three minutes. Trousseau is more specific. Check magnesium too.

line: Acetaminophen overdose antidote: N acetylcysteine.
sub: Best given within 8 hours of ingestion.
caption:
Acetaminophen overdose is treated with N acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione and binds the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Use the Rumack Matthew nomogram with a level drawn at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion. NAC works best when started within 8 hours but still helps later.

line: Opioid toxidrome: miosis, respiratory depression, altered mental status.
sub: The antidote is naloxone.
caption:
The opioid toxidrome is pinpoint pupils, slow or shallow breathing, and decreased level of consciousness. Treat the airway and breathing first, then give naloxone titrated to restore adequate breathing. Watch for recurrence because many opioids outlast naloxone.

line: Anticholinergic toxidrome: hot, dry, red, blind, and mad.
sub: Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter.
caption:
Anticholinergic toxicity gives fever, dry skin, flushing, dilated pupils, urinary retention, tachycardia, and delirium. Think diphenhydramine, tricyclics, and jimsonweed. Supportive care and benzodiazepines are the mainstay. Physostigmine is reserved for select cases.

line: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis.
sub: Hypotension, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation. Decompress.
caption:
Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed at the bedside: respiratory distress, hypotension, distended neck veins, and unilateral absent breath sounds, with tracheal deviation as a late sign. Do not wait for imaging. Decompress with needle or finger thoracostomy, then place a chest tube.

line: Kehr sign: left shoulder pain after abdominal trauma.
sub: Think splenic injury.
caption:
Kehr sign is pain in the left shoulder from blood irritating the diaphragm, referred through the phrenic nerve. In trauma, it suggests splenic injury. The same mechanism can cause right shoulder pain with liver or gallbladder problems.

line: Murphy sign: pain stops inspiration during RUQ palpation.
sub: Think acute cholecystitis.
caption:
Murphy sign is inspiratory arrest when you press under the right costal margin, because the inflamed gallbladder hits your hand. It suggests acute cholecystitis. Ultrasound findings include gallstones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy sign.

line: McBurney point: one third from the ASIS to the umbilicus.
sub: Classic tenderness in appendicitis.
caption:
McBurney point lies about one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Tenderness there is classic for appendicitis. Pain often starts around the umbilicus and migrates to the right lower quadrant. Imaging helps, and CT is common in adults.

line: Rovsing sign: pressing the LLQ causes pain in the RLQ.
sub: Supports appendicitis.
caption:
Rovsing sign is right lower quadrant pain when you palpate the left lower quadrant. It suggests peritoneal irritation from appendicitis. No single sign rules appendicitis in or out, so combine the exam with labs and imaging.

line: The most common ECG finding in PE is sinus tachycardia.
sub: S1Q3T3 is classic but uncommon.
caption:
In pulmonary embolism, the most common ECG finding is sinus tachycardia or nonspecific T wave changes. The classic S1Q3T3 pattern is seen in a minority of patients. A normal ECG does not rule out PE, so use pretest probability, D dimer when appropriate, and CT angiography.

line: Pheochromocytoma: episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations.
sub: Alpha blockade before beta blockade.
caption:
Pheochromocytoma causes episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, and hypertension from catecholamine release. Treat with alpha blockade first, such as phenoxybenzamine, before adding a beta blocker. Starting a beta blocker alone can cause unopposed alpha stimulation and a hypertensive crisis.

line: Adrenal crisis: hypotension, low sodium, high potassium, low glucose.
sub: Give hydrocortisone and fluids. Do not wait for labs.
caption:
Adrenal crisis presents with shock, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and often abdominal pain and vomiting. Think of it in patients on chronic steroids who miss doses or become acutely ill. Treat early with IV hydrocortisone and fluids, and look for the trigger.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: DKA: hold the insulin if potassium is below 3.3.
sub: Replace potassium first.
caption:
In DKA, total body potassium is low even if the serum level looks normal, because acidosis and insulin deficiency shift it out of cells. Insulin pushes potassium back in and can drop it dangerously. If potassium is below 3.3, replace it before starting insulin.

line: Glasgow Coma Scale: eyes 4, verbal 5, motor 6.
sub: Scores range from 3 to 15.
caption:
The Glasgow Coma Scale scores eye opening (up to 4), verbal response (up to 5), and motor response (up to 6), for a total of 3 to 15. A score of 8 or less is traditionally used as a threshold to consider securing the airway, but use clinical judgment.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: qSOFA: respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mentation, systolic BP 100 or less.
sub: Two or more flags higher risk of a poor outcome.
caption:
qSOFA is a quick bedside screen for patients with suspected infection who may deteriorate: respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mentation, and systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less. Two or more points flags higher risk. It is not a diagnostic test for sepsis, so a low score should never delay treatment. Think cultures, lactate, fluids, and early antibiotics.

line: NEXUS: five boxes that let you skip C spine imaging.
sub: No midline tenderness, no focal deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no painful distracting injury.
caption:
The NEXUS criteria identify low risk trauma patients who do not need cervical spine imaging. All five must be true: no midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurologic deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no painful distracting injury. If any one is missing, image. It does not apply to patients who are not evaluable.

line: Ottawa ankle rules: image only if pain plus a specific trigger.
sub: Can't take 4 steps, or bone tenderness at the back of a malleolus.
caption:
The Ottawa ankle rules reduce unnecessary X rays. Get an ankle series if there is pain near the malleoli and either bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the medial or lateral malleolus, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps both at injury and in the ED. For the foot, image if midfoot pain comes with tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular.

line: Subarachnoid hemorrhage: thunderclap headache, the worst of their life.
sub: A noncontrast CT within 6 hours is very sensitive.
caption:
Think subarachnoid hemorrhage with sudden maximal headache, often from a ruptured berry aneurysm. A noncontrast head CT read by a radiologist within 6 hours of onset is highly sensitive. If CT is negative but suspicion stays high, especially after 6 hours, do a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia or get a CT angiogram. Nimodipine helps prevent vasospasm complications.

line: Beta blocker overdose: slow heart, low pressure, sometimes low glucose.
sub: Glucagon is the classic first line antidote.
caption:
Beta blocker overdose causes bradycardia, hypotension, and sometimes hypoglycemia, especially in children. Glucagon raises cAMP by bypassing the blocked beta receptor. Other tools include IV fluids, atropine, calcium, vasopressors, and high dose insulin with glucose for refractory shock.

line: Calcium channel blocker overdose: give calcium, then high dose insulin.
sub: Look for high glucose with a slow heart and low pressure.
caption:
Calcium channel blocker overdose causes bradycardia and hypotension, and unlike beta blockers it often causes hyperglycemia because pancreatic insulin release depends on calcium channels. Treat with IV calcium, vasopressors, and high dose insulin with glucose. Lipid emulsion and ECMO are used in refractory cases.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Organophosphate poisoning: cholinergic toxidrome. Treat with atropine and pralidoxime.
sub: Titrate atropine until the lungs are dry.
caption:
Organophosphates block acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up. Expect salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, and fasciculations. Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects and is titrated to dry bronchial secretions. Pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme and works best when given early. Decontaminate and protect yourself.

Educational content only, not medical advice.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Carbon monoxide poisoning: the pulse ox looks normal, but oxygen delivery is not.
sub: Treat with 100 percent oxygen.
caption:
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen, and standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin. Use CO oximetry on a blood gas. Symptoms are headache, nausea, and confusion, and cherry red skin is uncommon. Treat with 100 percent oxygen, and consider hyperbaric therapy for loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits, ischemia, pregnancy, or very high levels.

line: Cyanide poisoning: think smoke inhalation. The antidote is hydroxocobalamin.
sub: Lactic acidosis with a high venous oxygen level.
caption:
Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase, so cells cannot use oxygen. Expect profound lactic acidosis, hypotension, seizures, and a high venous oxygen level. Think of enclosed space fires and nitroprusside. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form vitamin B12 and is the preferred antidote. Treat early without waiting for levels.

line: Methemoglobinemia: chocolate brown blood and a pulse ox stuck near 85 percent.
sub: Treat with methylene blue.
caption:
Methemoglobinemia happens when hemoglobin iron is oxidized and cannot carry oxygen. Triggers include benzocaine, dapsone, and nitrites. Clues are cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen and chocolate brown blood. Methylene blue is the antidote, but use caution in G6PD deficiency because it can cause hemolysis.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Salicylate toxicity: ringing ears, fast breathing, and a mixed acid base disorder.
sub: Alkalinize the urine. Dialysis if severe.
caption:
Aspirin overdose causes tinnitus, nausea, and fast breathing. The typical picture is respiratory alkalosis plus an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Give IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine and trap salicylate, and keep potassium normal. Avoid intubation if possible because losing the compensatory hyperventilation can be fatal. Dialysis is for altered mental status, severe acidosis, kidney failure, or very high levels.

line: Serotonin syndrome versus NMS: clonus and fast onset versus rigidity and slow onset.
sub: Cyproheptadine helps serotonin syndrome.
caption:
Serotonin syndrome develops within hours with hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor, diarrhea, and dilated pupils. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days with lead pipe rigidity, slowed reflexes, and fever after a dopamine antagonist. Stop the offending drug in both. Use benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, and dantrolene or bromocriptine for severe NMS.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Malignant hyperthermia: high fever and rigidity after anesthesia. Treat with dantrolene.
sub: Rising end tidal CO2 is an early sign.
caption:
Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine in susceptible patients, often with a ryanodine receptor defect. Early clues are rising end tidal CO2, rigidity, and tachycardia. Stop the trigger, give dantrolene to block calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cool the patient, and treat hyperkalemia.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM first, into the lateral thigh.
sub: Antihistamines and steroids are not first line.
caption:
Treat anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine right away, 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg per mL concentration, which is 0.3 to 0.5 mg for most adults, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes if needed. Add IV fluids, albuterol for bronchospasm, and monitor for a biphasic reaction. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not substitutes.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Status epilepticus: benzodiazepines first.
sub: Then a second line agent if seizures continue.
caption:
Treat a seizure lasting over 5 minutes as status epilepticus. Check glucose, protect the airway, and give a benzodiazepine first, such as IV lorazepam or IM midazolam. If seizures continue, give a second line agent like levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate. Refractory cases need anesthetic infusion and ICU care.

line: Ischemic stroke: check glucose, image, and consider alteplase within 4.5 hours.
sub: Thrombectomy can reach 24 hours in select patients.
caption:
In suspected stroke, check glucose first because hypoglycemia mimics stroke. Get a noncontrast head CT to exclude bleeding. IV alteplase is considered within 4.5 hours of last known well if no contraindications, with blood pressure below 185 over 110 before treatment. Thrombectomy for a large vessel occlusion can be considered up to 24 hours in selected patients.

line: Epidural hematoma: lens shaped, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval.
sub: Subdural is crescent shaped from bridging veins.
caption:
An epidural hematoma often follows temporal bone trauma that tears the middle meningeal artery. CT shows a biconvex, lens shaped collection. Patients may have a lucid interval before rapid deterioration. A subdural hematoma comes from torn bridging veins and appears crescent shaped, more often in older adults and alcohol use.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Aortic dissection: sudden tearing pain. Control the heart rate first.
sub: Beta blocker before a vasodilator.
caption:
Suspect aortic dissection with abrupt tearing chest or back pain, pulse or blood pressure differences between arms, or a widened mediastinum. Confirm with CT angiography. Lower the heart rate first with esmolol, aim for systolic blood pressure around 100 to 120, and add a vasodilator only after. Type A involves the ascending aorta and needs emergency surgery. Avoid anticoagulants and thrombolytics.

line: ST depression in V1 to V3? Think posterior MI.
sub: Check posterior leads V7 to V9.
caption:
Horizontal ST depression with tall R waves in V1 to V3 can be a posterior STEMI in disguise. Put leads on the back at V7 to V9, and ST elevation there confirms it. Treat as a STEMI with reperfusion. It often accompanies an inferior or lateral infarct.

line: Wellens syndrome: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2 and V3.
sub: Critical LAD stenosis. Avoid stress testing.
caption:
Wellens pattern appears in a pain free interval after chest pain and signals a critical proximal LAD lesion with a high risk of anterior MI. Cardiac enzymes may be normal or mildly elevated. Admit, start ACS treatment, and arrange angiography. Do not send the patient for a stress test.

line: Torsades de pointes: give IV magnesium, even if the level is normal.
sub: Defibrillate if unstable.
caption:
Torsades is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in the setting of a long QT interval. Causes include QT prolonging drugs, low potassium, and low magnesium. Give IV magnesium sulfate, correct potassium, and stop offending drugs. If pulseless or unstable, defibrillate. Overdrive pacing helps when it is bradycardia dependent.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: WPW with atrial fibrillation: avoid AV nodal blockers.
sub: Use procainamide or cardiovert.
caption:
In Wolff Parkinson White with atrial fibrillation, you see an irregular wide complex tachycardia. AV nodal blockers such as adenosine, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and digoxin can push more impulses down the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation. Use procainamide, or synchronized cardioversion if unstable.

line: Pericarditis on ECG: diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
sub: Pain eases leaning forward.
caption:
Pericarditis causes diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression and PR elevation in aVR, and pleuritic pain that improves sitting forward. Rule out STEMI, tamponade, and myocarditis before calling it benign. First line treatment is an NSAID plus colchicine.

line: Ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise in a woman of reproductive age with pain or bleeding.
sub: Positive hCG with no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound.
caption:
Always consider ectopic pregnancy in reproductive age women with abdominal pain, spotting, or syncope. Risk factors include prior ectopic, PID, tubal surgery, and IUD. Get a transvaginal ultrasound. If unstable with free fluid, go straight to the OR. Check Rh status and consider methotrexate only in stable patients who meet criteria.

line: Testicular torsion: sudden pain, high riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex.
sub: Surgical emergency. Salvage is best within 6 hours.
caption:
Torsion causes sudden severe scrotal pain, nausea, a high riding horizontal testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex. It peaks in adolescents. Do not delay urology for imaging if suspicion is high. Doppler ultrasound can help, and manual detorsion while arranging surgery can buy time. Salvage rates fall sharply after 6 hours.

line: Pyloric stenosis: projectile nonbilious vomiting at 2 to 6 weeks of age.
sub: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
caption:
Pyloric stenosis presents with hungry, projectile, nonbilious vomiting in a young infant, sometimes with an olive shaped mass. Labs show hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound confirms it. Correct fluids and electrolytes before pyloromyotomy.

line: Intussusception: colicky pain, currant jelly stool, sausage shaped mass.
sub: Ultrasound target sign. Air enema can treat it.
caption:
Intussusception peaks between 6 months and 3 years. Look for episodic drawing up of the legs, vomiting, and bloody mucus stool. Ultrasound shows a target sign. Air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic, and surgery is needed for perforation or failed reduction.

What systems, topics, pearls & tidbits would help you? Comment below.

line: Croup: barking cough and a steeple sign on neck X ray.
sub: Treat with dexamethasone.
caption:
Croup is usually from parainfluenza virus in children 6 months to 3 years, with a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor. A single dose of dexamethasone helps most children. Add nebulized epinephrine for stridor at rest and watch for rebound. Do not confuse with epiglottitis, where the child is toxic and drooling.

line: Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 days plus 4 of 5 findings.
sub: Conjunctivitis, rash, oral changes, extremity changes, cervical lymph node.
caption:
Kawasaki disease is a medium vessel vasculitis in young children. Fever for 5 days plus four of five features: bilateral conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, oral changes like strawberry tongue, hand and foot changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Treat with IVIG and aspirin, ideally within 10 days, to reduce coronary artery aneurysms. Get an echocardiogram.

line: Tumor lysis syndrome: high potassium, phosphate, and uric acid with low calcium.
sub: Hydrate aggressively. Rasburicase lowers uric acid.
caption:
Tumor lysis syndrome follows rapid cell death after chemotherapy, especially in leukemias and lymphomas. Cells release potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids, so you see hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia, with risk of kidney injury and arrhythmia. Treat with aggressive IV fluids, rasburicase, and management of hyperkalemia.

line: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia: platelets fall 5 to 10 days after heparin.
sub: Stop all heparin. Start argatroban or another nonheparin anticoagulant.
caption:
HIT is an immune reaction against heparin and platelet factor 4 that paradoxically causes clotting. Platelets typically fall 5 to 10 days after exposure, or sooner with recent exposure. Use the 4T score. Stop all heparin including flushes, start a nonheparin anticoagulant like argatroban, and avoid platelet transfusion and early warfarin.

line: TTP pentad: fever, anemia, low platelets, kidney injury, neurologic changes.
sub: Treat with plasma exchange.
caption:
TTP is caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, leading to microthrombi, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The smear shows schistocytes. Start plasma exchange urgently, along with steroids. Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is life threatening bleeding.

line: Neutropenic fever is an emergency: antibiotics within 60 minutes.
sub: Use an antipseudomonal beta lactam.
caption:
Neutropenic fever means fever in a patient with an absolute neutrophil count under 500, or expected to fall. Draw cultures but do not delay antibiotics. Give an antipseudomonal beta lactam such as cefepime, piperacillin tazobactam, or meropenem within 60 minutes. Risk stratify for admission and add coverage if unstable.

line: Bacterial meningitis: dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose.
sub: Empiric ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. Add ampicillin if over 50 or immunocompromised.
caption:
Do not delay antibiotics for imaging. If CT is needed before lumbar puncture, draw blood cultures and give antibiotics first. Standard empiric therapy is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, with ampicillin added to cover Listeria in older adults and immunocompromised patients. Dexamethasone given with or before the first dose reduces complications of pneumococcal meningitis.

line: Necrotizing fasciitis: pain out of proportion to the exam.
sub: Needs surgical exploration. Do not wait if unstable.
caption:
Necrotizing fasciitis causes severe pain, rapid spread, skin changes like bullae and crepitus, and systemic toxicity. Imaging or a risk score should not delay surgery when suspicion is high. Start broad antibiotics covering gram positives, gram negatives, and anaerobes, with clindamycin to reduce toxin production, and get the surgeon early.

line: Hypothermia on ECG: Osborn waves.
sub: J point elevation. Rewarm and handle gently.
caption:
Osborn waves are a positive deflection at the J point seen in significant hypothermia. Other findings include bradycardia, prolonged intervals, and arrhythmias. Handle the patient gently to avoid triggering ventricular fibrillation, rewarm actively, and continue resuscitation until the patient is warm.

line: Heat stroke: core temperature over 40 C with confusion.
sub: Cool first. Cold water immersion works best.
caption:
Heat stroke is a core temperature above about 40 C with central nervous system dysfunction, differentiating it from heat exhaustion. Rapid cooling decides outcome, and cold water immersion is the most effective method. Antipyretics do not work. Look for rhabdomyolysis, kidney injury, and liver injury.

line: Massive transfusion in trauma: balanced red cells, plasma, and platelets.
sub: Think 1 to 1 to 1.
caption:
Hemorrhagic shock is treated with balanced transfusion, close to 1 to 1 to 1 of red cells, plasma, and platelets. Add tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury and watch calcium. The goal is to break the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy, and to control bleeding quickly.

line: Light's criteria: a pleural effusion is exudative if the protein ratio is over 0.5.
sub: Or LDH ratio over 0.6, or pleural LDH over two thirds of the serum upper limit.
caption:
Light's criteria sort pleural effusions. An effusion is an exudate if pleural fluid protein to serum protein is over 0.5, pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH is over 0.6, or pleural fluid LDH is over two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Transudates are from heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome.

line: HHS: glucose over 600, serum osmolality over 320, minimal ketones.
sub: Fluids first.
caption:
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state causes extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration with little ketosis, usually in type 2 diabetes. Patients are often older and confused. Start with aggressive IV fluids, replace potassium, and give insulin once potassium is safe. Look for the trigger, such as infection or MI.

line: Thyroid storm: beta blocker, thionamide, then iodine one hour later.
sub: Add steroids and cooling.
caption:
Thyroid storm is severe hyperthyroidism with fever, tachycardia, agitation, and organ dysfunction. Give a beta blocker like propranolol, then a thionamide such as propylthiouracil, then iodine at least an hour later so it does not feed more hormone synthesis. Add hydrocortisone and cooling, and treat the trigger. Avoid aspirin.

line: Myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine plus IV hydrocortisone.
sub: Give steroids because adrenal insufficiency may coexist.
caption:
Myxedema coma is severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, and altered mental status. Hyponatremia is common. Give IV levothyroxine, and give IV hydrocortisone first or with it because of possible adrenal insufficiency. Support ventilation, rewarm passively, and treat the precipitant.

line: HEART score: History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin.
sub: Sorts low risk chest pain.
caption:
The HEART score helps risk stratify chest pain in the ED. A score of 0 to 3 is low risk, with a low chance of major adverse cardiac events at 6 weeks, and may allow early discharge. 4 to 6 is intermediate and 7 to 10 is high risk and needs admission and cardiology input.
